## Learning goals

The United States buys more from the rest of the world than it sells to it, and it has done so every year since
1976. Is that a problem? This chapter looks at the facts of trade and at a few small examples that explain why
countries trade at all. By the end of it you will be able to:

- read the U.S. trade data: exports, imports and the **trade balance** (net exports) as shares of GDP;
- derive $NX = S - I$ step by step from the national income identity $Y = C + I + G + NX$, explain why a trade
  deficit is borrowing from the rest of the world, and derive the country's **intertemporal budget constraint** and
  the long-run foreign debt ratio from the way deficits add up to a **foreign debt**;
- solve the textbook's trade examples with algebra (exchange, trade across time, **comparative advantage**, free
  migration), derive the free-trade world price and the condition for specialization, read the **comparative
  statics** as elasticities, and say who gains from each arrangement;
- compare trade balances across countries and periods, and check which year or which window a published number
  really refers to;
- go beyond the textbook's countries: pick any economy from World Bank, Penn World Table, IMF and External Wealth
  of Nations data, and check one source against another;
- in Python: write small accounting functions once and reuse them, reshape tables with `melt` and `pivot`, draw
  grouped bar charts, average over a window with `.loc[start:end]`, and add up flows with `cumsum`.

The next cell defines a helper that only the book website needs. Run it and move on.

```{python}
#| kind: helper
# @title Helper for the website versions (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def slider_figure(make_figure, name, values, start, label=None):
    """Precompute make_figure(name=value) for every value and join the results with one slider.

    The website cannot run Python, so each interactive figure also gets this precomputed version.
    """
    figures = [make_figure(**{name: v}) for v in values]
    first = values.index(start)
    fig = go.Figure(layout=figures[first].layout)
    owner = []                                  # which precomputed figure each trace comes from
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        for trace in f.data:
            trace.visible = (i == first)
            fig.add_trace(trace)
            owner.append(i)
    steps = []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        layout = {"title": f.layout.title.to_plotly_json(),
                  "annotations": [a.to_plotly_json() for a in f.layout.annotations],
                  "shapes": [s.to_plotly_json() for s in f.layout.shapes]}
        visible = [o == i for o in owner]
        steps.append(dict(method="update", label=str(values[i]), args=[{"visible": visible}, layout]))
    fig.update_layout(sliders=[dict(active=first, steps=steps, pad=dict(t=60),
                                    currentvalue=dict(prefix=(label or name) + " = "))])
    return fig
```

Every figure of this chapter can also show other countries. On the website, the many-country versions get a menu,
built by two more helpers.

```{python}
#| kind: helper
# @title Helpers for the many-country website versions (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
G7 = ["U.S.", "Japan", "Germany", "France", "United Kingdom", "Italy", "Canada"]
EMERGING = ["China", "India", "Brazil", "Russia", "Mexico", "Indonesia", "Türkiye", "South Africa",
            "Saudi Arabia", "Argentina"]


def country_groups(regions, book):
    """Menu groups: the textbook's countries, the G7, large emerging economies, then the World Bank regions."""
    groups = {"Textbook": list(book), "G7": G7, "Large emerging": EMERGING}
    for region in sorted(regions.region.unique()):
        groups[region] = list(regions[regions.region == region].country)
    return groups


def group_menu(fig, groups, start, title):
    """Show one group of countries at a time. A trace belongs to the country named before ', ' in its legendgroup.
    Each group gets a y range that covers its values; in groups of more than 15 countries it leaves out extreme
    outliers (double-click the chart to show them)."""
    owners = [t.legendgroup.split(", ")[0] for t in fig.data]
    buttons = []
    for name, members in groups.items():
        visible = [o in members for o in owners]
        ys = np.concatenate([np.asarray(t.y, dtype=float) for t, v in zip(fig.data, visible) if v] or [np.zeros(1)])
        ys = ys[np.isfinite(ys)] if np.isfinite(ys).any() else np.zeros(1)
        lo, hi = ys.min(), ys.max()
        if len(set(o for o, v in zip(owners, visible) if v)) > 15:     # large groups: leave out extreme outliers
            q5, q95 = np.percentile(ys, [5, 95])
            lo, hi = max(lo, q5 - 0.3 * (q95 - q5)), min(hi, q95 + 0.3 * (q95 - q5))
        pad = 0.06 * (hi - lo) + 0.5
        buttons.append(dict(label=name, method="update",
                            args=[{"visible": visible}, {"yaxis.range": [lo - pad, hi + pad], "yaxis.autorange": False}]))
    first = list(groups).index(start)
    for t, v in zip(fig.data, buttons[first]["args"][0]["visible"]):
        t.visible = v
    fig.update_layout(title=title, yaxis_range=buttons[first]["args"][1]["yaxis.range"], yaxis_tickvals=None,
                      margin=dict(t=115), updatemenus=[dict(buttons=buttons, active=first, direction="down",
                                                             x=0, y=1.02, xanchor="left", yanchor="bottom")])
    return fig
```

## Model overview

Why do countries trade with each other, and what does it mean when a country buys more from abroad than it sells? This chapter answers with two kinds of tools. The first is a set of **accounting identities**: rules that hold by definition, in every country and every year. They tie exports and imports to saving, investment, the government budget and the stock of foreign debt, so that every trade chart below can be read as a statement about lending and borrowing. The second is a set of small **trade models**, economies simple enough to solve with pencil and paper, that show where the gains from trade come from and who receives them.

The road map has two parts. We build the accounting first: the trade balance and the national income identity, then its saving–investment form, then the stock of net foreign assets and the budget constraint that a country faces over time. Then come four small models: two islands that swap two goods, two islands that lend to each other across time, a North and a South that trade by **comparative advantage**, and free migration as an alternative to trade in goods. At the end, `### The model in code` writes each rule once as a Python function, recomputes the textbook's tables of the trade examples and checks every result with numbers. The figure sections reuse these functions.

A word on notation. Capital letters are flows of goods during a year: output $Y$, consumption $C$, investment $I$, government purchases $G$, taxes $T$, exports $EX$, imports $IM$, net exports $NX$ and saving $S$. Lower-case letters are the same flows as fractions of GDP, such as $c = C/Y$ or $nx = NX/Y$. A bar marks a parameter chosen from outside, such as the interest rate $\bar{r}$ or the growth rate $\bar{g}$. In the North–South model the subscripts $n$ and $s$ stand for North and South, and the productivities $x$ and $z$ and the labor forces $L$ are fixed numbers.

<!-- cell -->

### The trade balance and the national income identity

#### Definitions

- **Exports** $EX$ are goods and services produced at home and sold to buyers abroad. **Imports** $IM$ are goods and services produced abroad and bought by households, firms or the government at home.
- The **trade balance**, also called **net exports**, is the difference $NX \equiv EX - IM$. A positive value is a trade **surplus**, a negative value a trade **deficit**.
- A flow $X$ as a **share of GDP** is $100 \times X/Y$ ([Appendix C.2](https://quarcs-lab.github.io/macro102-site/notebooks/appC-math-review-for-macroeconomics.html#c.2-percentages-ratios-and-index-numbers)). Shares let us put a small and a large economy, or 1950 and 2025, on the same axis.
- The **national income identity** splits production into its uses: $Y = C + I + G + NX$. Why net exports and not exports? Spending $C + I + G$ includes goods made abroad, which are not part of domestic production, so imports are subtracted. Goods made at home and sold abroad are part of production but appear in no domestic spending, so exports are added. Hence $Y = (C + I + G) + EX - IM$.

#### Solving the identity

**Step 1: net exports as production minus domestic spending.** Subtract $C + I + G$ from both sides of the identity:

$$NX = Y - (C + I + G). \tag{1}$$

The sum $C + I + G$ is everything that households, firms and the government use at home, sometimes called **domestic absorption**. Equation (1) gives two cases:

$$NX < 0 \;\Longleftrightarrow\; C + I + G > Y, \qquad\qquad NX > 0 \;\Longleftrightarrow\; C + I + G < Y.$$

*Intuition.* A country with a trade deficit uses more goods than it makes. The extra goods arrive from abroad, and since nobody hands goods over for free, they come with a promise to pay later. A country with a surplus sends part of its output abroad and collects such promises. When a deficit country pays back, the inequality has to flip: for a while it must make more than it uses.

**Step 2: the same identity in GDP shares.** Divide every term of equation (1) by $Y$:

$$\frac{NX}{Y} = \frac{Y}{Y} - \frac{C}{Y} - \frac{I}{Y} - \frac{G}{Y}
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad nx = 1 - c - i - g. \tag{2}$$

The Penn World Table reports the shares $c$, $i$ and $g$ but not $nx$, so equation (2) is how we get the trade balances of Figs. 3 and 4. For example, $c = 0.55$, $i = 0.25$ and $g = 0.18$ add up to $0.98$, which leaves a surplus of 2 percent of GDP.

**Step 3: the world as a whole.** Split the world into two regions, the United States (US) and the rest of the world (RoW). Each U.S. import is a rest-of-world export and each U.S. export is a rest-of-world import, $IM_{US} = EX_{RoW}$ and $EX_{US} = IM_{RoW}$. Therefore

$$NX_{US} = EX_{US} - IM_{US} = IM_{RoW} - EX_{RoW} = -NX_{RoW}.$$

The world trades only with itself, so the trade balances of all countries add up to zero. To see which countries cover the U.S. deficit, both sides must be measured against the same GDP. Multiplying and dividing by country $j$'s GDP $Y_j$ gives

$$\frac{NX_j}{Y_{US}} = \frac{NX_j}{Y_j}\times\frac{Y_j}{Y_{US}}.$$

This is the second bar of Fig. 3. A surplus of 2 percent of its own GDP in an economy three quarters the size of the United States covers $2 \times 0.75 = 1.5$ percent of U.S. GDP.

#### What the identity predicts

An identity does not tell us what causes what. It tells us which combinations of numbers can occur together. For a given level of output $Y$:

| A change in ... | effect on the trade balance |
|---|---|
| $C$, $I$ or $G$ up by 1 | $NX$ down by 1 |
| $c + i + g$ up by 1 point of GDP | $nx$ down by 1 point |
| U.S. deficit up by 1 point of U.S. GDP | surpluses elsewhere up by 1 point of U.S. GDP in total |

All three effects are one for one, because the identity is a sum. The direction of cause is open: a spending boom at home can open a deficit, and cheap credit from abroad can also feed a spending boom. The models below and the data sections look at which story fits.

<!-- cell -->

### Saving, investment and the trade balance

#### Definitions

- **Private saving** is income after taxes minus consumption, $Y - T - C$. Here $T$ is taxes net of transfers, as in [Chapter 18](https://quarcs-lab.github.io/macro102-site/notebooks/ch18-the-government-and-the-macroeconomy.html).
- **Government saving** is the budget surplus, $T - G$. It is negative when the government runs a deficit.
- **Foreign saving** is $IM - EX = -NX$: the goods that the rest of the world sends us beyond what we send back, which is lending to us.
- **Domestic saving** adds the first two: $S \equiv (Y - T - C) + (T - G)$.

#### Solving the identity

**Step 1.** Solve the national income identity for investment: $I = Y - C - G - NX$.

**Step 2.** Subtract and add taxes, which changes nothing: $I = (Y - T - C) + (T - G) - NX$.

**Step 3.** Write $-NX$ as $IM - EX$:

$$I = \underbrace{(Y - T - C)}_{\text{private saving}} + \underbrace{(T - G)}_{\text{government saving}} + \underbrace{(IM - EX)}_{\text{foreign saving}}. \tag{3}$$

Every unit of investment is paid for by one of three savers: households, the government or foreigners.

**Step 4.** The taxes cancel inside domestic saving, $S = (Y - T - C) + (T - G) = Y - C - G$. So Step 1 reads $I = S - NX$. Moving $NX$ to the left and $I$ to the right:

$$\underbrace{NX}_{\text{trade balance}} = \underbrace{S - I}_{\text{net capital outflow}}. \tag{4}$$

*Intuition.* Equation (4) describes one set of transactions in two ways. On the goods side, a country with $NX < 0$ receives more goods than it ships. On the financial side, it saves less than it invests, $S < I$, and the difference is lent to it by foreigners, who receive bonds, shares or dollars in return. **Net capital outflow** $S - I$ is the net amount that a country lends to the rest of the world. A trade deficit and net borrowing from abroad are the same thing, seen from the goods side and from the financial side.

**Step 5: the twin deficits.** Split domestic saving into its two parts:

$$NX = \underbrace{(Y - T - C - I)}_{\text{private saving minus investment}} + \underbrace{(T - G)}_{\text{government saving}}.$$

If private saving and investment stay roughly in line, the first term is close to zero, and the trade balance moves with the budget balance: a budget deficit comes with a trade deficit of about the same size. These are the **twin deficits** of Fig. 5.

#### What the identity predicts

Equation (4) holds in every year, but it does not say which term adjusts. The table lists the possible cases, each for a change of 1 point of GDP:

| A change in ... | holding fixed ... | effect |
|---|---|---|
| budget deficit $G - T$ up | private saving and $I$ | $NX$ down by 1: the twin deficits |
| budget deficit $G - T$ up | private saving and $NX$ | $I$ down by 1: crowding out at home |
| investment $I$ up | $S$ | $NX$ down by 1: foreigners finance it |
| private saving up | $I$ and $T - G$ | $NX$ up by 1: the country lends abroad |

Two implications for the data sections. A fast-growing country with a high investment rate can still run a trade surplus if its saving is even higher, as in China (Fig. 4). And the large U.S. budget deficits of the 1980s and 2000s were paired mostly with larger trade deficits rather than with lower investment (Fig. 5).

<!-- cell -->

### Net foreign assets and the intertemporal budget constraint

#### Definitions

- **Net foreign assets** $F_t$ are what a country's residents own abroad minus what foreigners own in the country, at the end of year $t$. The data call it the **net international investment position** (Fig. 6). When $F_t < 0$, minus $F_t$ is the **net foreign debt**.
- The **current account** adds to the trade balance the net income earned on foreign assets: $CA_t \equiv NX_t + \bar{r}F_{t-1}$, where $\bar{r}$ is the return on foreign assets. (The data also include remittances and aid, which we leave out.) The textbook's trade examples ignore this income, so in them the current account and the trade balance are the same.

#### Solving the model

**Step 1: assets accumulate the current account.** A current account surplus is new lending to the rest of the world, so it raises the stock of foreign assets by the same amount:

$$F_t - F_{t-1} = NX_t + \bar{r}F_{t-1} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad F_t = (1 + \bar{r})F_{t-1} + NX_t. \tag{5}$$

This is a **difference equation** ([Appendix C.10](https://quarcs-lab.github.io/macro102-site/notebooks/appC-math-review-for-macroeconomics.html#c.10-difference-equations-how-macro-variables-move-over-time)). With $\bar{r} = 0$, as in the island example below and in the dotted line of Fig. 6, it becomes $F_t = F_{t-1} + NX_t$, so that $F_t = F_0 + NX_1 + NX_2 + \dots + NX_t$: the stock is the starting stock plus the sum of all trade balances since.

**Step 2: the budget constraint over many years.** Divide both sides of equation (5) by $(1 + \bar{r})^t$, and use $(1 + \bar{r})/(1 + \bar{r})^t = 1/(1 + \bar{r})^{t-1}$:

$$\frac{F_t}{(1 + \bar{r})^t} = \frac{F_{t-1}}{(1 + \bar{r})^{t-1}} + \frac{NX_t}{(1 + \bar{r})^t}.$$

Write this line for $t = 1, 2, \dots, T$ and add all the lines. Each term $F_t/(1+\bar{r})^t$ from $t = 1$ to $T - 1$ appears once on the left and once on the right, so it cancels, and only the two ends survive:

$$\frac{F_T}{(1 + \bar{r})^T} = F_0 + \sum_{t=1}^{T}\frac{NX_t}{(1 + \bar{r})^t}.$$

No lender lets a debt grow forever without repayment, and no country gives goods to the world forever without ever using the claims. So, looking far enough ahead, the present value of the final stock is zero, $F_T/(1 + \bar{r})^T = 0$. Then

$$\sum_{t=1}^{T}\frac{NX_t}{(1 + \bar{r})^t} = -F_0. \tag{6}$$

This is the country's **intertemporal budget constraint**. The terms on the left are present values ([Appendix C.12](https://quarcs-lab.github.io/macro102-site/notebooks/appC-math-review-for-macroeconomics.html#c.12-present-value-and-discounting)). The math is the same as for the government's budget constraint in [Chapter 18](https://quarcs-lab.github.io/macro102-site/notebooks/ch18-the-government-and-the-macroeconomy.html), but it now applies to the whole country.

*Intuition.* A country that starts with no foreign assets, $F_0 = 0$, must run trade balances whose present value is zero: every deficit today has to be matched by surpluses later, worth as much in present value. A country that starts as a debtor, $F_0 < 0$, has to run surpluses on average.

**Step 3: the foreign debt as a share of GDP.** Let GDP grow at the rate $\bar{g}$, so that $Y_t = (1 + \bar{g})Y_{t-1}$, and write $f_t \equiv F_t/Y_t$. Divide equation (5) by $Y_t$:

$$f_t = \frac{(1 + \bar{r})F_{t-1}}{(1 + \bar{g})Y_{t-1}} + \frac{NX_t}{Y_t} = \frac{1 + \bar{r}}{1 + \bar{g}}\,f_{t-1} + nx_t.$$

If GDP grows faster than the return, $\bar{g} > \bar{r}$, the coefficient on $f_{t-1}$ is below one and, for a constant trade balance $nx$, the ratio settles down. In the long run $f_t = f_{t-1} = f^*$, so $f^* - \frac{1 + \bar{r}}{1 + \bar{g}}f^* = nx$, that is $f^*\,\frac{\bar{g} - \bar{r}}{1 + \bar{g}} = nx$, and

$$f^* = \frac{(1 + \bar{g})\,nx}{\bar{g} - \bar{r}}. \tag{7}$$

Both $F$ and $Y$ are in dollars here, so $\bar{g}$ is the growth rate of nominal GDP. A deficit of 3 percent of GDP every year, with nominal GDP growing 4 percent and no net income on foreign assets, leads to $f^* = 1.04 \times (-0.03)/0.04 = -0.78$: a net foreign debt of 78 percent of GDP. The U.S. debt of about 70 percent of GDP in Fig. 6 is of that order.

#### What the model predicts

- **Deficits are borrowing, and they add up.** By equation (5), the foreign debt is roughly the sum of past current account deficits. Fig. 6 tests this. It also shows that the data have one more source of change: the value of foreign assets moves with stock prices and the dollar.
- **Trade must balance over time, in present value.** By equation (6), no country can run deficits forever. A deficit is a promise of future surpluses, not a free gift of goods.
- **Comparative statics of the debt ratio**, from equation (7):

| A rise in ... | effect on the long-run ratio $f^*$ | with $nx = -0.03$, $\bar{g} = 0.04$, $\bar{r} = 0$ |
|---|---|---|
| the deficit $-nx$, by 1 point | debt up by $(1+\bar{g})/(\bar{g}-\bar{r})$ points; the elasticity with respect to $nx$ is 1 | about 26 points more debt |
| the growth rate $\bar{g}$ | debt ratio smaller: the same deficit is spread over a larger economy | $\bar{g} = 0.05$: debt of 63 percent instead of 78 |
| the return $\bar{r}$ (below $\bar{g}$) | debt ratio larger: interest on the debt adds to the borrowing | $\bar{r} = 0.02$: debt of 156 percent |

<!-- cell -->

### Gains from exchange: two islands, two goods

#### Assumptions

1. Two islands have the same population. Each person likes bananas and fish, and only in equal amounts: think of a meal as one banana with one fish.
2. Nothing is produced. Each year, every person on island 1 receives 200 bananas and 800 fish, and every person on island 2 the reverse, 800 bananas and 200 fish.
3. The two goods can be swapped between the islands. By symmetry, they swap one for one.

#### Solving the model

Without trade, a person on island 1 can put together only $\min(200, 800) = 200$ meals: the 600 extra fish add nothing. Suppose island 1 swaps $q$ fish for $q$ bananas. It then holds $200 + q$ bananas and $800 - q$ fish. Equal amounts require

$$200 + q = 800 - q \quad\Longrightarrow\quad 2q = 600 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad q = 300.$$

Each person on both islands ends with 500 bananas and 500 fish. In general, with endowments $(a, b)$ on one island and $(b, a)$ on the other, the swap is $q = (b - a)/2$, and everyone ends with $(a + b)/2$ of each good.

#### What the model predicts

- **Both islands gain.** Meals per person rise from 200 to 500 on each island, although nothing more is produced. The gain comes only from moving each good to the people who value it more at the margin.
- **Trade here is balanced.** In every year each island ships as much as it receives, so $NX = 0$. The next block shows how deficits and surpluses arise.
- **Trade between countries works like trade between people.** Inside a country, people specialize and buy most of what they consume from others. Trade across borders extends the same idea.

<!-- cell -->

### Trade across time: Oddtopia and Eventopia

#### Assumptions

1. There is one good, wheat, and it cannot be stored from one year to the next.
2. Oddtopia harvests 100 bushels in odd years and nothing in even years. Eventopia has the opposite pattern.
3. People prefer a smooth path of consumption to a path that swings: because of diminishing marginal utility, the last bushel eaten in a good year is worth less than the first bushel in a bad year (the consumption smoothing of [Chapter 16](https://quarcs-lab.github.io/macro102-site/notebooks/ch16-consumption.html)).
4. There is no investment and no government, $I = G = 0$. An island that lends wheat is paid back the same amount a year later, so $\bar{r} = 0$. Both islands start with no foreign assets, $F_0 = 0$.

#### Solving the model

**Step 1: the trade balance.** With $I = G = 0$, equation (1) becomes $NX_t = Y_t - C_t$: the harvest minus what is eaten.

**Step 2: consumption.** The two islands together harvest 100 bushels every year. Wheat cannot be stored, so the 100 bushels are eaten within the year, and the smoothest split of a constant total that is also the same each year is 50 bushels for each island: $C_t = 50$.

**Step 3: the trade balances.** For Oddtopia, $NX_t = 100 - 50 = +50$ in odd years and $NX_t = 0 - 50 = -50$ in even years. Eventopia's trade balance is the exact mirror image, so the two balances add to zero in every year, as Step 3 of the first block requires.

**Step 4: the assets.** By equation (5) with $\bar{r} = 0$ and $F_0 = 0$, Oddtopia's net foreign assets are $F_1 = 50$, $F_2 = 50 - 50 = 0$, $F_3 = 50$, and so on: after each good year it holds a claim of 50 bushels on Eventopia, which is repaid the next year. Eventopia's assets are $-50, 0, -50, \dots$

**Step 5: the budget constraint.** With $\bar{r} = 0$ and $F_0 = 0$, equation (6) says that the trade balances must add up to zero. Over any two years they do: $+50 - 50 = 0$.

#### What the model predicts

- **Risk sharing.** Each island eats 50 bushels every year, even though its harvest swings between 0 and 100. Without trade it would feast and starve in turns.
- **A deficit can be good news for welfare.** Each island runs a deficit exactly when its harvest fails. The deficit is a loan that lets it keep eating.
- **Balanced on average.** Each island's average trade balance is zero, in line with equation (6). A deficit today is the counterpart of a surplus tomorrow.
- **A guide for the data.** The same logic says that a country should borrow, and run deficits, when its income is temporarily low, when it expects to grow faster than the rest of the world, or when it has good investment projects. Fig. 4 asks whether fast-growing countries really borrow.

### Comparative advantage: the North and the South

#### Assumptions

1. Two countries, the North ($n$) and the South ($s$), produce and consume two goods, apples and computers. Labor is the only input, and each worker supplies one unit of labor for a wage $w$, which is the worker's whole income.
2. In country $j$, a worker can make either $x_j$ apples or $z_j$ computers, and there are $L_j$ workers. The values used throughout this notebook are those of the textbook's example:

| | North | South |
|---|---|---|
| workers $L$ | 100 | 400 |
| apples per worker $x$ | 160 | 100 |
| computers per worker $z$ | 16 | 2 |

3. Workers can switch freely between the two sectors of their own country, but they cannot cross the border (the migration block below drops this assumption).
4. Everyone spends half of income on apples and half on computers. Prices are measured in apples (the **numéraire**): an apple costs 1, and a computer costs $p$ apples. With $c_A$ and $c_C$ the apples and computers that one person consumes, the two spending shares give

$$\frac{1 \times c_A}{w} = \frac{1}{2} \;\;\text{and}\;\; \frac{p \times c_C}{w} = \frac{1}{2}
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad c_A = \frac{w}{2}, \qquad c_C = \frac{w}{2p}. \tag{8}$$

The North is more productive in both goods, $x_n > x_s$ and $z_n > z_s$: it has an **absolute advantage** in both. But its lead is much larger in computers, $z_n/z_s = 16/2 = 8$, than in apples, $x_n/x_s = 160/100 = 1.6$. Cross-multiplying, $z_n/z_s > x_n/x_s$ is the same as $x_s/z_s > x_n/z_n$: the number of apples given up to make one computer is $160/16 = 10$ in the North and $100/2 = 50$ in the South. A computer is relatively cheaper to make in the North, so the North has a **comparative advantage** in computers, and the South in apples.

#### Solving the model: autarky

Under **autarky**, each country is closed to trade.

**Step 1: the wage.** A worker in the apple sector makes $x$ apples, and an apple costs 1, so the wage is $w = x$.

**Step 2: the price of a computer.** A worker in the computer sector makes $z$ computers and earns $p\,z$ apples. People want both goods, so both sectors must hire workers, and then both must pay the same: $p\,z = x$. If $p\,z$ were higher, every worker would move to computers and nobody would grow apples; if lower, nobody would make computers. So

$$w = x, \qquad p = \frac{x}{z}. \tag{9}$$

The price of a computer equals its **opportunity cost**, the apples given up to make it ([Appendix C.9](https://quarcs-lab.github.io/macro102-site/notebooks/appC-math-review-for-macroeconomics.html#c.9-solving-equations-and-systems) on solving such conditions).

**Step 3: consumption.** Put equation (9) into equation (8): $c_A = x/2$ and $c_C = \dfrac{x/2}{x/z} = \dfrac{z}{2}$.

**Step 4: who works where.** The $L_A$ workers in the apple sector make $L_A\,x$ apples, and the $L$ people eat $L\,x/2$. Setting the two equal gives $L_A = L/2$: half of the workers make apples and half make computers.

With our numbers, the North has $w = 160$, $p = 10$, $c_A = 80$ and $c_C = 8$, and it makes $50 \times 160 = 8{,}000$ apples and $50 \times 16 = 800$ computers. The South has $w = 100$, $p = 50$, $c_A = 50$ and $c_C = 1$, and it makes $200 \times 100 = 20{,}000$ apples and $200 \times 2 = 400$ computers.

#### Solving the model: free trade

**Step 1: arbitrage.** Under autarky a computer costs 10 apples in the North and 50 in the South. A trader could buy computers in the North and sell them in the South at a profit (**arbitrage**). With free trade there is one world price $p$.

**Step 2: a guess.** Suppose each country makes only the good of its comparative advantage: the North only computers and the South only apples. The world then makes $L_n z_n = 1{,}600$ computers and $L_s x_s = 40{,}000$ apples.

**Step 3: the world price.** World income, measured in apples, is the value of everything produced, $L_s x_s + p\,L_n z_n$. Half of it is spent on computers, and in equilibrium the computers bought equal the computers made:

$$p\,L_n z_n = \tfrac{1}{2}\left(L_s x_s + p\,L_n z_n\right)
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \tfrac{1}{2}\,p\,L_n z_n = \tfrac{1}{2}\,L_s x_s
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad p = \frac{L_s x_s}{L_n z_n}. \tag{10}$$

With equal spending shares, the two goods must have the same total value, so the price of a computer is the ratio of world apples to world computers: $40{,}000/1{,}600 = 25$ apples.

**Step 4: wages.** A southern worker still makes 100 apples, so $w_s = x_s = 100$. A northern worker makes 16 computers worth 25 apples each, so $w_n = p\,z_n = 400$ apples. Using equation (10), $w_n = L_s x_s/L_n$.

**Step 5: consumption.** By equation (8): in the North, $c_A = 400/2 = 200$ and $c_C = 400/(2 \times 25) = 8$; in the South, $c_A = 100/2 = 50$ and $c_C = 100/(2 \times 25) = 2$.

**Step 6: check the guess.** Northern workers stay in computers only if that pays at least as well as apples, $p\,z_n \ge x_n$, that is $p \ge x_n/z_n$. Southern workers stay in apples only if $x_s \ge p\,z_s$, that is $p \le x_s/z_s$. With strict inequalities, complete specialization requires

$$\frac{x_s}{z_s} \;>\; p = \frac{L_s x_s}{L_n z_n} \;>\; \frac{x_n}{z_n}. \tag{11}$$

The world price must lie between the two autarky prices. Here $50 > 25 > 10$, so the guess is right. If, say, the South were so large that $p$ rose above 50, southern workers would also make some computers, and the South would keep its autarky price.

#### What the model predicts

**Both countries gain, for any numbers that satisfy (11).** Compare each item of consumption under autarky and free trade:

| | autarky | free trade | comparison |
|---|---|---|---|
| North, apples | $x_n/2 = 80$ | $p\,z_n/2 = 200$ | higher, because $p > x_n/z_n$ |
| North, computers | $z_n/2 = 8$ | $w_n/(2p) = z_n/2 = 8$ | the same |
| South, apples | $x_s/2 = 50$ | $x_s/2 = 50$ | the same |
| South, computers | $z_s/2 = 1$ | $x_s/(2p) = 2$ | higher, because $p < x_s/z_s$ |

Each country gets more of the good it imports and no less of the good it makes. Trade rests on **comparative** advantage: the North gains even though it is better at everything. World output rises too, from $28{,}000$ apples and $1{,}200$ computers under autarky to $40{,}000$ apples and $1{,}600$ computers.

**Comparative statics.** Taking logs of the free-trade results ([Appendix C.4](https://quarcs-lab.github.io/macro102-site/notebooks/appC-math-review-for-macroeconomics.html#c.4-logarithms)), for example $\ln p = \ln L_s + \ln x_s - \ln L_n - \ln z_n$, gives each elasticity as a coefficient. They hold as long as condition (11) holds:

| A 1% rise in ... | $p = \frac{L_s x_s}{L_n z_n}$ | $w_n$, North apples $= \frac{L_s x_s}{2L_n}$ | North computers $= \frac{z_n}{2}$ | South apples $= \frac{x_s}{2}$ | South computers $= \frac{L_n z_n}{2L_s}$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $z_n$ (northern computers) | $-1\%$ | $0$ | $+1\%$ | $0$ | $+1\%$ |
| $x_s$ (southern apples) | $+1\%$ | $+1\%$ | $0$ | $+1\%$ | $0$ |
| $L_n$ (northern workers) | $-1\%$ | $-1\%$ | $0$ | $0$ | $+1\%$ |
| $L_s$ (southern workers) | $+1\%$ | $+1\%$ | $0$ | $0$ | $-1\%$ |

A better computer technology in the North makes computers cheaper all over the world. The North's wage in apples does not change, because each computer now buys fewer apples, and the South gains as much in computers as the North does. Productivity gains are shared through prices. For example, with $z_n = 20$ the world price falls to $40{,}000/2{,}000 = 20$ apples, and condition (11) still holds, $50 > 20 > 8$.

<!-- cell -->

### Free migration: moving workers instead of goods

#### Assumptions

Keep the North–South model, but now let workers move across the border. Technologies stay where they are: a worker in the North makes $x_n$ apples or $z_n$ computers, wherever he or she was born. Production has constant returns, so output per worker does not depend on how many workers a country has.

#### Solving the model

**Step 1: who moves.** With free trade a computer costs the same everywhere, so a higher wage in apples is a higher real wage. The northern wage, 400 apples, is four times the southern one, 100 apples (under autarky it is 160 against 100). Southern workers keep moving as long as any gap remains. Because the North is more productive in *both* goods, a worker makes more of either good there, and the South empties out.

**Step 2: the new world economy.** The world is now the North under autarky, with $L_n + L_s = 500$ workers. By equation (9), $w = x_n = 160$ and $p = x_n/z_n = 10$. By equation (8), everybody eats $c_A = 80$ apples and has $c_C = 8$ computers.

**Step 3: production.** Half of the 500 workers make each good: $250 \times 160 = 40{,}000$ apples and $250 \times 16 = 4{,}000$ computers.

#### What the model predicts

- **Migration follows absolute advantage**, while trade in goods follows comparative advantage. Workers go where productivity is highest in absolute terms.
- **The world produces more** than with free trade: the same 40,000 apples, and 4,000 computers instead of 1,600.
**The gains go to the migrants.** What one worker consumes under each arrangement:

| | autarky | free trade | free migration |
|---|---|---|---|
| a worker born in the North | 80 apples, 8 computers | 200 apples, 8 computers | 80 apples, 8 computers |
| a worker born in the South | 50 apples, 1 computer | 50 apples, 2 computers | 80 apples, 8 computers |

Northern workers are back at their autarky bundle, because with constant returns the newcomers do not change their productivity. So northerners prefer free trade to free migration.

- **There is room to compensate the North.** Moving from free trade to free migration, each of the 100 northerners loses 120 apples, 12,000 apples in all. Each of the 400 migrants gains 30 apples and 6 computers, 12,000 apples and 2,400 computers in all. The gains are larger than the losses. If every migrant handed 30 apples to the North, each northerner would get back exactly the free-trade bundle of 200 apples and 8 computers, and each migrant would still have 50 apples and 8 computers, four times the computers of free trade.
- **Moving labor versus moving capital.** The production and Solow models ([Chapter 4](https://quarcs-lab.github.io/macro102-site/notebooks/ch04-a-model-of-production.html), [Chapter 5](https://quarcs-lab.github.io/macro102-site/notebooks/ch05-the-solow-growth-model.html)) found that poor countries are poor mostly because of low total factor productivity, not because of too little capital. Sending capital to a low-productivity economy leaves that problem in place. Letting workers move to where productivity is high attacks it directly, which is why the possible gains from migration are so large.
- **The costs of trade.** In the model, apple growers in the North become computer makers overnight and nobody loses. In reality, switching jobs takes time and new skills, so trade creates winners and losers inside each country. Because the gains to the winners are larger than the losses, the winners could, in principle, compensate the losers, for example through retraining and a social safety net.

### The model in code

We now turn the accounting rules into Python functions, check each derivation above with numbers, and recompute the textbook's tables for the trade examples. Each function's description names the equation it computes. The figure sections reuse these functions.

> **Python note.** `def` creates a *function*: a named recipe that takes inputs (the *arguments*) and gives back a
> result with `return`. The text in triple quotes is a short description. The same function works for single
> numbers and for whole columns of a data table, because pandas does arithmetic on every row at once.

```{python}
def share_of_gdp(x, gdp):
    """Any variable as a percent of GDP: 100 x / Y."""
    return 100 * x / gdp


def net_exports(exports, imports):
    """The trade balance (net exports): NX = EX - IM."""
    return exports - imports


def net_exports_from_uses(Y, C, I, G):
    """The national income identity solved for net exports: NX = Y - (C + I + G)   (equation 1)."""
    return Y - (C + I + G)


def trade_balance_share(c, i, g):
    """NX as a percent of GDP from the GDP shares of C, I and G: 100 (1 - c - i - g)   (equation 2)."""
    return 100 * net_exports_from_uses(1, c, i, g)


def share_of_us_gdp(share, gdp, gdp_us):
    """Rescale a share of a country's own GDP to a share of U.S. GDP (Fig. 19.3, second bar)."""
    return share * gdp / gdp_us
```

Four more functions handle saving and the data over time: two forms of equation (4), an **average over a window of
years**, and the **sum of past flows**, which turns yearly trade balances into a stock of foreign assets or debt
(equation 5 with $\bar{r} = 0$).

> **Python note.** For a table whose rows are years, `data.loc[start:end]` keeps the rows from `start` to `end`,
> both included, and `.mean()` averages them (one average per column). `.cumsum()` is the *cumulative sum*: row by
> row, the sum of all values so far.

```{python}
def domestic_saving(I, NX):
    """Domestic saving S = Y - C - G, from equation (4): S = I + NX."""
    return I + NX


def net_capital_outflow(S, I):
    """Equation (4): the trade balance equals domestic saving minus investment, NX = S - I."""
    return S - I


def period_average(data, start, end):
    """Simple average over the years start to end (rows are years): one number per column."""
    return data.loc[start:end].mean()


def accumulate(start_value, flows):
    """Net foreign assets with no interest: start from start_value and add each year's trade balance (equation 5)."""
    return start_value + flows.cumsum()
```

#### Checking the accounting

**Check 1: equations (1) to (4).** An economy produces 100, consumes 70, invests 20, its government buys 15 and
collects 12 in taxes. Each identity must give the same trade balance.

```{python}
Y, C, I, G, T = 100, 70, 20, 15, 12
NX = net_exports_from_uses(Y, C, I, G)
print(f"Equation (1): NX = {Y} - ({C} + {I} + {G}) = {NX}, or {share_of_gdp(NX, Y):.0f}% of GDP")
print(f"Equation (2): 100 (1 - c - i - g) = {trade_balance_share(C / Y, I / Y, G / Y):.1f}% of GDP")
private, government, foreign = Y - T - C, T - G, -NX
print(f"Equation (3): private {private} + government {government} + foreign {foreign} "
      f"= {private + government + foreign}, and I = {I}")
S = private + government
print(f"Equation (4): S - I = {S} - {I} = {net_capital_outflow(S, I)}, the same as NX = {NX}")
print(f"... and back again: S = I + NX = {domestic_saving(I, NX)}")
print(f"Domestic uses C + I + G = {C + I + G} > Y = {Y}: a trade deficit")
```

**Check 2: the world adds up to zero.** The United States runs a deficit of 3 (in goods) and the rest of the world,
three times as large, runs the matching surplus.

```{python}
gdp_us, gdp_row = 100, 300
NX_us = -3
NX_row = -NX_us                                  # every U.S. import is a rest-of-world export
row_share = share_of_gdp(NX_row, gdp_row)
print(f"World trade balance: {NX_us + NX_row}")
print(f"Rest of the world: a surplus of {row_share:.0f}% of its own GDP, "
      f"or {share_of_us_gdp(row_share, gdp_row, gdp_us):.0f}% of U.S. GDP")
```

**Check 3: the intertemporal budget constraint.** A country with no foreign assets borrows 50 in year 1 and repays
the loan with 5 percent interest in year 2. Equation (5) should bring its assets back to zero, and the present value
of its two trade balances should be zero, as equation (6) says.

> **Python note.** `range(1, 3)` counts 1, 2. A list is numbered from 0, so `trade_balance[t - 1]` is the trade
> balance of year `t`. `x = x + ...` replaces the old value of `x` with the new one.

```{python}
r = 0.05
trade_balance = [-50, 50 * (1 + r)]              # borrow 50, then repay 50 plus interest
F = 0.0                                          # no foreign assets at the start
present_value = 0.0
for t in range(1, 3):
    F = (1 + r) * F + trade_balance[t - 1]                     # equation (5)
    present_value = present_value + trade_balance[t - 1] / (1 + r) ** t
    print(f"Year {t}: NX = {trade_balance[t - 1]:+.1f}, F = {F:+.2f}")
print(f"Present value of the trade balances = {present_value:.6f}   (equation 6: -F0 = 0)")
```

**Check 4: the long-run debt ratio.** We apply the ratio form of equation (5) year after year with a constant
deficit of 3 percent of GDP, and compare where it ends with the formula of equation (7).

```{python}
def debt_ratio_steady_state(nx, g, r=0.0):
    """Long-run net foreign assets as a share of GDP: f* = (1 + g) nx / (g - r)   (equation 7)."""
    return (1 + g) * nx / (g - r)


for g, r in [(0.04, 0.0), (0.05, 0.0), (0.04, 0.02)]:
    f = 0.0                                          # start with no foreign assets
    for year in range(1000):
        f = (1 + r) / (1 + g) * f + (-0.03)          # equation (5) divided by GDP
    print(f"g = {g:.0%}, r = {r:.0%}: simulated f = {100 * f:.1f}% of GDP, "
          f"formula = {100 * debt_ratio_steady_state(-0.03, g, r):.1f}%")
```

#### Gains from exchange: the banana-and-fish islands

> **Python note.** `min(a, b)` is the smaller of two numbers: the number of complete meals.

```{python}
bananas_1, fish_1 = 200, 800                     # island 1, per person
bananas_2, fish_2 = 800, 200                     # island 2, per person
q = (fish_1 - bananas_1) / 2                     # fish that island 1 swaps for bananas, one for one
print(f"Island 1 swaps {q:.0f} fish for {q:.0f} bananas")
print(f"Island 1 eats {bananas_1 + q:.0f} bananas and {fish_1 - q:.0f} fish; "
      f"island 2 eats {bananas_2 - q:.0f} bananas and {fish_2 + q:.0f} fish")
print(f"Meals per person on island 1: {min(bananas_1, fish_1)} without trade, "
      f"{min(bananas_1 + q, fish_1 - q):.0f} with trade")
```

#### Trade across time: Oddtopia and Eventopia (Table 19.1)

With no investment and no government, equation (1) gives $NX = Y - C$, the harvest minus what is eaten. The sum of
past trade balances (equation 5 with $\bar{r} = 0$) is what the other island owes.

> **Python note.** `pd.DataFrame({...})` builds a table from a *dictionary* of columns. The `for` loop repeats the
> indented lines for each island, and `island + " harvest"` glues two pieces of text into a column name. `.T`
> turns the table on its side, so that the years become columns, as in the textbook.

```{python}
wheat = pd.DataFrame({"year": [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6],
                      "Oddtopia harvest": [100, 0, 100, 0, 100, 0],
                      "Eventopia harvest": [0, 100, 0, 100, 0, 100]})
for island in ["Oddtopia", "Eventopia"]:
    wheat[island + " consumption"] = 50                    # half of the world harvest, every year
    wheat[island + " trade balance"] = net_exports_from_uses(wheat[island + " harvest"],
                                                             wheat[island + " consumption"], 0, 0)
    wheat[island + " is owed"] = accumulate(0, wheat[island + " trade balance"])
wheat.set_index("year").T
```

```{python}
book_balance = [50, -50, 50, -50, 50, -50]                 # Oddtopia's row of Table 19.1
same = (wheat["Oddtopia trade balance"] == book_balance).all()
print(f"Oddtopia's trade balance equals Table 19.1: {same}")
world = wheat["Oddtopia trade balance"] + wheat["Eventopia trade balance"]
print(f"The two trade balances add to zero in every year: {(world == 0).all()}")
for island in ["Oddtopia", "Eventopia"]:
    print(f"{island}: sum of trade balances {wheat[island + ' trade balance'].sum()} (equation 6 with r = 0), "
          f"consumption always {wheat[island + ' consumption'].iloc[0]}")
```

#### Comparative advantage: the North and the South (Tables 19.2 to 19.5)

```{python}
x_n, z_n, L_n = 160, 16, 100        # North: apples or computers per worker, number of workers (Table 19.2)
x_s, z_s, L_s = 100, 2, 400         # South
print(f"North / South productivity: apples {x_n / x_s:.1f} times, computers {z_n / z_s:.0f} times")
print(f"Apples given up for one computer: North {x_n / z_n:.0f}, South {x_s / z_s:.0f}")
```

**Autarky.** The function follows Steps 1 to 4 of the autarky solution.

> **Python note.** `pd.Series({...})` builds a list of numbers with labels from a dictionary. `pd.DataFrame` then
> puts two such lists side by side as the columns "North" and "South". `pd.concat([...], axis=1, keys=[...])`
> places two tables next to each other under two headings.

```{python}
def autarky(x, z, L):
    """Table 19.3: a closed economy whose L workers each make x apples or z computers."""
    w = x                        # the wage in apples: what a worker makes in the apple sector (equation 9)
    p = x / z                    # the price of a computer: both sectors must pay the same wage (equation 9)
    return pd.Series({"Wage, w (apples)": w,
                      "Price of a computer, p (apples)": p,
                      "Apples per person": w / 2,              # equation (8): an apple costs 1
                      "Computers per person": w / 2 / p,       # equation (8)
                      "Workers making apples (%)": 50,
                      "Workers making computers (%)": 50,
                      "Apples produced": L / 2 * x,
                      "Computers produced": L / 2 * z})


table_19_3 = pd.DataFrame({"North": autarky(x_n, z_n, L_n), "South": autarky(x_s, z_s, L_s)})
book_19_3 = pd.DataFrame({"North": [160, 10, 80, 8, 50, 50, 8000, 800],
                          "South": [100, 50, 50, 1, 50, 50, 20000, 400]}, index=table_19_3.index)
pd.concat([table_19_3, book_19_3], axis=1, keys=["Notebook", "Textbook"])
```

**Free trade.** The function follows Steps 2 to 5 of the free-trade solution: complete specialization, the world
price of equation (10), the wages and consumption from equation (8).

```{python}
def free_trade(x_n, z_n, L_n, x_s, z_s, L_s):
    """Table 19.4: the North makes only computers, the South only apples, and they trade."""
    computers = L_n * z_n                      # world production of computers
    apples = L_s * x_s                         # world production of apples
    p = apples / computers                     # equation (10): half of world spending goes to each good
    w_n, w_s = z_n * p, x_s                    # wages in apples
    north = pd.Series({"Wage, w (apples)": w_n, "Price of a computer, p (apples)": p,
                       "Apples per person": w_n / 2, "Computers per person": w_n / 2 / p,
                       "Workers making apples (%)": 0, "Workers making computers (%)": 100,
                       "Apples produced": 0, "Computers produced": computers})
    south = pd.Series({"Wage, w (apples)": w_s, "Price of a computer, p (apples)": p,
                       "Apples per person": w_s / 2, "Computers per person": w_s / 2 / p,
                       "Workers making apples (%)": 100, "Workers making computers (%)": 0,
                       "Apples produced": apples, "Computers produced": 0})
    return pd.DataFrame({"North": north, "South": south})


table_19_4 = free_trade(x_n, z_n, L_n, x_s, z_s, L_s)
table_19_4
```

The textbook's Table 19.4 has the same numbers: a world price of 25 apples, a northern wage of 400 apples, and
consumption of 200 apples and 8 computers in the North and 50 apples and 2 computers in the South. Two checks: both
world markets clear, and condition (11) holds, so complete specialization really is the outcome.

```{python}
demand_computers = (table_19_4.loc["Computers per person"] * [L_n, L_s]).sum()
demand_apples = (table_19_4.loc["Apples per person"] * [L_n, L_s]).sum()
print(f"Computers: demand {demand_computers:,.0f} = supply {table_19_4.loc['Computers produced'].sum():,.0f}")
print(f"Apples:    demand {demand_apples:,.0f} = supply {table_19_4.loc['Apples produced'].sum():,.0f}")
p_world = table_19_4.loc["Price of a computer, p (apples)", "North"]
print(f"Condition (11): autarky price South {x_s / z_s:.0f} > world price {p_world:.0f} > autarky price North "
      f"{x_n / z_n:.0f}: {x_s / z_s > p_world > x_n / z_n}")
print(f"World output: {table_19_3.loc['Apples produced'].sum():,.0f} apples and "
      f"{table_19_3.loc['Computers produced'].sum():,.0f} computers under autarky, "
      f"{table_19_4.loc['Apples produced'].sum():,.0f} and {table_19_4.loc['Computers produced'].sum():,.0f} with trade")
```

**Check: the elasticities.** Raise northern computer productivity $z_n$ by 1 percent. The comparative-statics table
predicts $-1\%$ for the world price, $0$ for the northern wage and for apples per person in both countries, and $+1\%$
for computers per person in both countries.

```{python}
better = free_trade(x_n, z_n * 1.01, L_n, x_s, z_s, L_s)
items = [("Price of a computer, p (apples)", "North"), ("Wage, w (apples)", "North"),
         ("Apples per person", "North"), ("Computers per person", "North"),
         ("Apples per person", "South"), ("Computers per person", "South")]
for item in items:
    row, country = item
    change = better.loc[row, country] / table_19_4.loc[row, country] - 1
    print(f"{country}, {row}: {100 * change:+.2f}%")
```

The price falls by 0.99 percent rather than exactly 1 percent, because an elasticity describes very small changes.

**Free migration.** If workers can move instead of goods, every southern worker moves to the North, where wages are
higher. The world then looks like the North under autarky, with all 500 workers (Table 19.5).

```{python}
migration = autarky(x_n, z_n, L_n + L_s)
table_19_5 = pd.DataFrame({"Born in the North": migration, "Migrants from the South": migration})
table_19_5
```

Who gains? The next table compares what one worker consumes under the three arrangements.

```{python}
regimes = {"Autarky": table_19_3, "Free trade": table_19_4,
           "Free migration": pd.DataFrame({"North": migration, "South": migration})}
rows = []
for name in regimes:
    t = regimes[name]
    rows.append([name, t.loc["Apples per person", "North"], t.loc["Computers per person", "North"],
                 t.loc["Apples per person", "South"], t.loc["Computers per person", "South"]])
pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["Regime", "North: apples", "North: computers", "South: apples", "South: computers"])
```

**Check: compensating the North.** Each migrant hands 30 apples to the North. Northerners should get back their
free-trade bundle, migrants should still beat theirs, and the world's apples and computers should be enough for all.

```{python}
fee = 30                                                       # apples per migrant
north_apples = migration["Apples per person"] + fee * L_s / L_n
migrant_apples = migration["Apples per person"] - fee
computers_each = migration["Computers per person"]
print(f"Northerner: {north_apples:.0f} apples, {computers_each:.0f} computers "
      f"(free trade: {table_19_4.loc['Apples per person', 'North']:.0f} and "
      f"{table_19_4.loc['Computers per person', 'North']:.0f})")
print(f"Migrant:    {migrant_apples:.0f} apples, {computers_each:.0f} computers "
      f"(free trade: {table_19_4.loc['Apples per person', 'South']:.0f} and "
      f"{table_19_4.loc['Computers per person', 'South']:.0f})")
print(f"Apples eaten {L_n * north_apples + L_s * migrant_apples:,.0f} = apples produced "
      f"{migration['Apples produced']:,.0f}")
```

Change a number in the productivity cell (for example `z_n = 20`) and run the cells again to see how the tables
change, and compare the changes with the comparative-statics table above.

## Some basic facts about trade

We begin with the U.S. numbers: how much the country sells abroad and buys from abroad, and how the gap between the two has grown since the 1970s. Then we put the United States next to the rest of the world.

<!-- cell -->

### Fig. 1: U.S. import and export shares of GDP

**Goal.** See how much more the United States trades today than 75 years ago.

The file `us_trade.csv` holds the U.S. national accounts we need, in billions of current dollars: GDP, exports,
imports, net exports, private investment and the **net international investment position** (Fig. 6), plus the
same position as it was published in July 2023.

> **Python note.** `set_index("year")` makes the years the row labels, so that `us.loc[2006]` is the row of 2006
> and `us.exports` is one column, a *Series* with years as labels. `NaN` ("not a number") marks a missing value:
> the investment position starts only in 1976.

```{python}
us = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "us_trade.csv").set_index("year")
us.tail()
```

We turn exports and imports into shares of GDP with our function `share_of_gdp`, and check the result against the
figure's own data file.

```{python}
shares = pd.DataFrame({"Exports": share_of_gdp(us.exports, us.gdp),
                       "Imports": share_of_gdp(us.imports, us.gdp)})
check = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig19-1.csv").set_index("year")
print(f"Largest difference from fig19-1.csv: {(shares.Exports - check.exports_share).abs().max():.4f} points")
shares.loc[[1950, 1957, 1976, 2006, 2022, 2025]].round(2)
```

> **Python note.** `px.line` with a list `y=[...]` draws one line per column. Instead of a legend, the textbook
> writes the names next to the lines: `fig.add_annotation` puts a text at a point, and `yshift` moves it up or down
> by a number of pixels.

```{python}
first, last = shares.index[0], shares.index[-1]
fig = px.line(shares.reset_index(), x="year", y=["Exports", "Imports"], color_discrete_sequence=[BLUE, GREEN],
              labels={"year": "Year", "value": "Percent of GDP", "variable": "Series"},
              title=f"{first}–{last}: U.S. exports rose from {shares.Exports[first]:.1f}% to "
                    f"{shares.Exports[last]:.1f}% of GDP, imports from {shares.Imports[first]:.1f}% to "
                    f"{shares.Imports[last]:.1f}%")
fig.update_traces(line_width=3)
fig.add_annotation(x=last, y=shares.Imports[last], text="Imports", showarrow=False, xanchor="left", xshift=6,
                   font=dict(size=15, color=GREEN))    # labels at the end of each line
fig.add_annotation(x=last, y=shares.Exports[last], text="Exports", showarrow=False, xanchor="left", xshift=6,
                   font=dict(size=15, color=BLUE))
fig.update_layout(showlegend=False)
fig.update_xaxes(range=[1948, 2033])
fig.update_yaxes(range=[2, 18.5], tickvals=[4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16, 18])
fig.show()
```

**Sources.** Data: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA), National Income and Product Accounts, via FRED: [Exports of goods and services (`EXPGSA`)](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/EXPGSA),
[Imports of goods and services (`IMPGSA`)](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/IMPGSA) and [Gross domestic product (`GDPA`)](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/GDPA).
Prepared file: [`data/ch19/us_trade.csv`](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch19/us_trade.csv), checked against [`data/ch19/fig19-1.csv`](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch19/fig19-1.csv) (see the [data notes](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch19/README.md)).
Chart: inspired by Fig. 19.1 in Jones (2024), [*Macroeconomics*, 6th ed.](https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324063612)

<!-- cell -->

**What to notice.**

- In the 1950s exports and imports were each only about 4 to 5 percent of GDP. Since then exports have more than
  doubled and imports more than tripled.
- The two lines move together until the early 1970s, and then they separate: imports have been above exports every
  year since 1976. The gap between them is the trade deficit of Fig. 2.
- Trade falls sharply in world recessions (2009, 2020) and in the strong-dollar years of the mid-1980s, when U.S.
  exports dropped to 7 percent of GDP.

<!-- cell -->

#### Key numbers: how much does the United States trade?

The textbook says that exports and imports rose "from under 5 percent of GDP in the 1950s to around 12 and 15
percent of GDP, respectively, in recent years" (Jones 2024).

> **Python note.** `~` means "not": `~above` is True in the years when imports were **not** above exports.
> `.idxmax()` gives the label (here the year) of the largest value.

```{python}
fifties = shares.loc[1950:1959]
print(f"1950s: highest export share {fifties.Exports.max():.2f}% ({fifties.Exports.idxmax()}), "
      f"highest import share {fifties.Imports.max():.2f}%")
print(f"2022, the textbook's last year: exports {shares.Exports[2022]:.2f}%, imports {shares.Imports[2022]:.2f}%")
above = shares.Imports > shares.Exports
print(f"Imports have been above exports every year since {above[~above].index.max() + 1}")
openness = shares.Exports + shares.Imports
print(f"Exports + imports: {openness[1950]:.1f}% of GDP in 1950, {openness.max():.1f}% at the peak "
      f"({openness.idxmax()}), {openness[last]:.1f}% in {last}")
```

The textbook's "respectively" lists the two numbers the wrong way round: exports are about 12 percent of GDP
(11.65 percent in 2022) and imports about 15 percent (15.18 percent). And "under 5 percent" holds only after rounding: exports
reached 5.07 percent in 1957. Exports and imports together, a common measure of how **open** an economy is, went
from 8 percent of GDP in 1950 to a peak of 30.8 percent in 2011.

<!-- cell -->

#### Beyond the United States: how open is each economy?

The textbook shows only the United States. The World Bank's *World Development Indicators* (WDI) publish the same
two shares, exports and imports of goods and services as a percent of GDP (series `NE.EXP.GNFS.ZS` and
`NE.IMP.GNFS.ZS`), for almost every economy. The file `wdi_trade.csv` has one row per economy and year from 1960 to
2025 (most economies start later, and 2025 is still missing for many). Its column `trade_balance` is exports minus
imports (`NE.RSB.GNFS.ZS`), which we use in Fig. 2. The small file `countries.csv` gives each economy's World Bank
region and income group.

> **Python note.** `.nunique()` counts the different values in a column. Subtracting two Series lines them up by
> their labels (here the years), and a year that one of them lacks gives `NaN`, which `.max()` skips. For the
> United States the WDI copy the BEA's numbers, so the two sources should agree.

```{python}
world = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "wdi_trade.csv")         # World Bank WDI, percent of GDP
regions = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "countries.csv")       # World Bank region and income group of each economy
us_wdi = world[world.country == "U.S."].set_index("year")
gap = max((us_wdi.exports - shares.Exports).abs().max(), (us_wdi.imports - shares.Imports).abs().max())
print(f"{world.country.nunique()} economies, {world.year.min()}-{world.year.max()}; the U.S. rows start in "
      f"{us_wdi.index.min()} and differ from the BEA data by at most {gap:.2f} points")
world.head()
```

Each economy gets one fixed color, so that it keeps its color when you add or remove others. Plotly offers 44 dark
enough colors, fewer than the 214 economies, so `group_colors` hands them out such that the economies of one menu
group (the G7, a region, ...) never share a color, as far as 44 colors allow.

```{python}
LIGHT = ["#F7E1A0", "#E2E2E2", "#FBE426", "#16FF32", "#1CFFCE", "#2ED9FF"]     # too pale on a white background
PALETTE = []
for color in px.colors.qualitative.Dark24 + px.colors.qualitative.Alphabet:   # 24 + 26 colors, 44 of them kept
    if color not in LIGHT and color != "#2E91E5":
        PALETTE.append(color)
PALETTE.append("#2E91E5")                       # Dark24's medium blue goes last: it is close to the book's navy
```

> **Python note.** For each country, `score` gives every color a cost: 1 for each country that already uses it, 10
> for each one in a large group (Europe has more countries than there are colors) and 100 for each one in a group
> small enough to avoid any clash. `a if test else b` gives `a` when the test is True. `min(PALETTE, key=score.get)`
> picks the color with the lowest cost (the first one on ties). When no color is free, `PALETTE[::-1]` (the list in
> reverse order) makes the search start from the end of the list, so that the leftovers take the last, rarely used
> colors.

```{python}
def group_colors(names, groups, fixed=None):
    """A color for each country that no other country in its groups uses, as far as the palette allows.

    groups: the lists of countries shown together (the menu views); fixed: the textbook countries' colors."""
    colors = dict(fixed or {})
    for name in sorted(names):
        if name in colors:
            continue
        score = {}                                  # the cost of each color: lower is better
        for color in PALETTE:
            score[color] = list(colors.values()).count(color)            # 1 per country using it anywhere
        for group in groups:
            if name in group:
                weight = 100 if len(group) <= len(PALETTE) else 10      # a clash in a small group costs most
                for other in group:
                    if colors.get(other) in score:
                        score[colors[other]] += weight
        best = min(PALETTE, key=score.get)                              # the cheapest color
        if score[best] >= 10:                       # no free color: the least used one, searching from the end
            best = min(PALETTE[::-1], key=score.get)
        colors[name] = best
    return colors


COLORS = group_colors(regions.country, country_groups(regions, ["U.S."]).values(), {"U.S.": BLUE})
```

The dictionary `COLORS` maps each economy to its color, and `color_discrete_map=COLORS` makes Plotly use it, in Colab
and on the website. `fit_range` keeps the textbook's axis range when the data fit in it; otherwise it returns `None`,
which lets Plotly choose a range that shows every value.

```{python}
def fit_range(values, book_range):
    """The textbook's axis range if every value fits in it, otherwise None (Plotly then chooses)."""
    if values.min() >= book_range[0] and values.max() <= book_range[1]:
        return book_range
    return None
```

The figure function draws Fig. 19.1 for any list of economies. The title reports exports plus imports, the
**openness** of each economy, in its latest year.

> **Python note.** `.melt(...)` stacks the export and import columns into one column `share`, with a new column
> `flow` that says which is which; `line_dash="flow"` then draws exports solid and imports dashed.
> `.groupby("country").last()` keeps each economy's last row. `", ".join(names)` glues a list of texts together, and
> `a if test else b` gives `a` when the test is True and `b` otherwise: the title names two economies and counts
> the rest.

```{python}
FLOWS = {"Exports and imports": ["Exports", "Imports"], "Exports": ["Exports"], "Imports": ["Imports"]}


def trade_shares_world(countries=("U.S.",), flow="Exports and imports"):
    """Fig. 19.1 for any economies: exports and imports, percent of GDP (World Bank WDI)."""
    rows = world[world.country.isin(countries)].rename(columns={"exports": "Exports", "imports": "Imports"})
    if len(rows) == 0:
        return go.Figure(layout=dict(title="Choose at least one economy"))
    long = rows.melt(id_vars=["country", "year"], value_vars=FLOWS[flow], var_name="flow", value_name="share")
    last = rows.dropna(subset=["Exports", "Imports"]).groupby("country").last()
    names = []
    for name in last.index[:2]:
        names.append(f"{name} {last.Exports[name] + last.Imports[name]:.0f}%")
    more = f" + {len(last) - 2} more" if len(last) > 2 else ""
    fig = px.line(long, x="year", y="share", color="country", line_dash="flow", hover_name="country",
                  color_discrete_map=COLORS, labels={"year": "Year", "share": "Percent of GDP", "flow": "Flow"},
                  title="Latest exports + imports, % of GDP: " + ", ".join(names) + more)
    fig.update_traces(line_width=3)
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[1955, 2027])         # 1960 sits away from the corner
    fig.update_yaxes(range=fit_range(long.share.dropna(), [2, 18.5]))
    fig.update_layout(legend_title_text="")
    return fig
```

> **Python note.** `SelectMultiple` is a list from which you can choose several items: hold Ctrl (Cmd on a Mac)
> and click. Its `value` is the list chosen at the start, here only the United States, as in the textbook.

```{python}
#| kind: widget
interact(trade_shares_world,
         countries=SelectMultiple(options=sorted(world.country.unique()), value=["U.S."], rows=8,
                                  description="economies", style=WIDE),
         flow=ToggleButtons(options=list(FLOWS), value="Exports and imports", description="flows"));
```

```{python}
#| kind: website
# @title Website version: exports and imports of every economy, one group at a time
fig = trade_shares_world(tuple(world.country.unique()), "Exports and imports")
group_menu(fig, country_groups(regions, ["U.S."]), "Textbook",
           "Exports (solid) and imports (dashed), percent of GDP: choose a group in the menu")
```

**Sources.** Data: World Bank, World Development Indicators: [Exports of goods and services, % of GDP (`NE.EXP.GNFS.ZS`)](https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/NE.EXP.GNFS.ZS) and
[Imports of goods and services, % of GDP (`NE.IMP.GNFS.ZS`)](https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/NE.IMP.GNFS.ZS); World Bank, [country and lending groups](https://datahelpdesk.worldbank.org/knowledgebase/articles/906519-world-bank-country-and-lending-groups) (regions and income groups of the menus).
Prepared files: [`data/ch19/wdi_trade.csv`](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch19/wdi_trade.csv) and [`data/ch19/countries.csv`](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch19/countries.csv) (see the [data notes](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch19/README.md)).
Chart: inspired by Fig. 19.1 in Jones (2024), [*Macroeconomics*, 6th ed.](https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324063612)

*On the website, the menu above the chart shows one group of economies at a time; click a name in the legend to hide
it, and double-click the chart to show extreme values that the chosen range leaves out.*

How open is the United States compared with other economies?

```{python}
in_2024 = world[world.year == 2024].set_index("country")
openness_2024 = (in_2024.exports + in_2024.imports).sort_values()
rank = list(openness_2024.index).index("U.S.") + 1
print(f"In 2024 the U.S. is number {rank} of {len(openness_2024)} economies, counting from the least open")
openness_2024.loc[["U.S.", "Brazil", "China", "Japan", "India", "Germany", "Ireland", "Singapore"]].round(1)
```

The United States is one of the **least open** economies in the world: in 2024 only four of 172 economies traded
less relative to their GDP. Large economies trade less, because much of their trade happens inside their own
borders. Small trading hubs such as Singapore (313 percent) and Luxembourg (351 percent) import goods and
re-export them, so their exports and imports can each exceed GDP.

### Fig. 2: The U.S. trade balance as a share of GDP

**Goal.** Measure the U.S. trade deficit and test the rule that trade must balance in the long run.

The trade balance is exports minus imports. We compute it with `net_exports`, turn it into a share of GDP, and check
it against the figure's data file, which was computed from the BEA's own net-exports series.

```{python}
us["trade_balance"] = share_of_gdp(net_exports(us.exports, us.imports), us.gdp)
check = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig19-2.csv").set_index("year")
print(f"Largest difference from fig19-2.csv: {(us.trade_balance - check.trade_balance_pct_gdp).abs().max():.4f} points")
us.trade_balance.loc[[1950, 1975, 1976, 1987, 2006, 2025]].round(2)
```

The Oddtopia example says that the trade balance must average zero over a long period. The figure function shades a
window of years and reports the average trade balance in it, using our `period_average`.

> **Python note.** `min(a, b)` and `max(a, b)` give the smaller and the larger of two numbers, so the window stays
> valid even if the two sliders cross. `(series < 0).sum()` counts the years with a deficit, because each True
> counts as 1. `add_vrect` shades a band between two x values, and `add_shape(type="line", ...)` draws a segment.

```{python}
def trade_balance_chart(start=1976, end=2025):
    """Fig. 19.2: the U.S. trade balance (% of GDP), with its average from start to end."""
    start, end = min(start, end), max(start, end)         # in case the sliders cross
    avg = period_average(us.trade_balance, start, end)
    deficits = (us.trade_balance.loc[start:end] < 0).sum()
    fig = px.line(us.reset_index(), x="year", y="trade_balance", color_discrete_sequence=[BLUE],
                  labels={"year": "Year", "trade_balance": "Percent of GDP"},
                  title=f"{start}–{end}: average trade balance {avg:+.2f}% of GDP, "
                        f"deficits in {deficits} of {end - start + 1} years")
    fig.update_traces(line_width=3)
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_dash="dash", line_color="black", line_width=1)
    fig.add_vrect(x0=start, x1=end, fillcolor=GRAY, opacity=0.15, line_width=0)
    fig.add_shape(type="line", x0=start, x1=end, y0=avg, y1=avg, line=dict(color=TEAL, width=3, dash="dot"))
    fig.add_annotation(x=1990, y=1.6, text="Above zero: exports > imports", showarrow=False, font=dict(size=13))
    fig.add_annotation(x=1965, y=-4.5, text="Below zero: imports > exports", showarrow=False, font=dict(size=13))
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[1948, 2027])
    fig.update_yaxes(range=[-6.5, 2.5], tickvals=[-5, -4, -3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2])   # no label in the corner
    return fig
```

> **Python note.** `interact` turns each argument of the function into a widget and draws the figure again whenever
> you move one. `IntSlider` is a slider for whole numbers. The `;` at the end only hides an extra line of text.

```{python}
#| kind: widget
interact(trade_balance_chart,
         start=IntSlider(value=1976, min=1950, max=2025, step=1, description="first year", style=WIDE),
         end=IntSlider(value=2025, min=1950, max=2025, step=1, description="last year", style=WIDE));
```

```{python}
#| kind: website
# @title Website version: Fig. 2 with a precomputed slider for the first year (last year 2025)
slider_figure(trade_balance_chart, "start", [1950, 1960, 1976, 1990, 2000, 2010], start=1976, label="first year")
```

**Sources.** Data: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA), National Income and Product Accounts, via FRED: [Exports of goods and services (`EXPGSA`)](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/EXPGSA),
[Imports of goods and services (`IMPGSA`)](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/IMPGSA), [Gross domestic product (`GDPA`)](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/GDPA) and
[Net exports of goods and services (`A019RC1A027NBEA`)](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/A019RC1A027NBEA).
Prepared file: [`data/ch19/us_trade.csv`](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch19/us_trade.csv), checked against [`data/ch19/fig19-2.csv`](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch19/fig19-2.csv) (see the [data notes](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch19/README.md)).
Chart: inspired by Fig. 19.2 in Jones (2024), [*Macroeconomics*, 6th ed.](https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324063612)

<!-- cell -->

**What to notice.**

- From 1950 to 1975 the United States usually had a small surplus (the dotted average line is above zero for that
  window). After 1975 the pattern reversed: there has not been a single surplus year since.
- The deficit grew in two waves, to about 3 percent of GDP in 1987 and to 5.7 percent in 2006, and has stayed near
  3 percent since 2009. The dotted line is the average over the shaded years.
- Over the whole period 1950–2025 the average is still negative, about −1.5 percent of GDP. Trade has not
  balanced yet: according to the Oddtopia example, the rest of the world expects future U.S. surpluses.

<!-- cell -->

#### Key numbers: the deficit in the text

```{python}
tb = us.trade_balance
early = tb.loc[1950:1975]
print(f"1950-1975: surplus in {(early > 0).sum()} of {len(early)} years; deficits in {list(early[early < 0].index)}")
print(f"Surplus years after 1975: {list(tb.loc[1976:][tb.loc[1976:] > 0].index)}")
print(f"Largest deficit: {tb.min():.2f}% of GDP in {tb.idxmin()}")
print(f"2000-2022: from {tb.loc[2000:2022].min():.2f}% to {tb.loc[2000:2022].max():.2f}% of GDP")
print(f"Average 2023-2025: {period_average(tb, 2023, 2025):.2f}% of GDP")
print(f"2006: domestic uses C + I + G were {100 - tb[2006]:.1f}% of GDP (equation 1)")
```

The text's numbers hold: a surplus in 23 of the 26 years from 1950 to 1975, no surplus since, a deficit of 5.7
percent in 2006 (the text says 5.6; the data have been revised since) and about 3 percent in recent years. In 2006,
Americans consumed, invested and bought through their governments 105.7 percent of what they produced.

<!-- cell -->

#### Beyond the United States: who runs deficits, who runs surpluses?

Does trade balance in the long run in other countries? The same figure, for any economy, uses the WDI trade balance
of `wdi_trade.csv`. The dotted lines are each economy's average over the chosen years.

> **Python note.** `go.Scatter(x=[start, end], y=[avg, avg], mode="lines")` draws one straight segment.
> `legendgroup=name` ties it to the economy's line, so that a click on the legend hides both, and
> `showlegend=False` keeps it out of the legend.

```{python}
def add_average(fig, series, name, start, end):
    """Draw the average of a yearly series from start to end as a dotted segment, and return the average."""
    avg = period_average(series, start, end)
    if avg == avg:                                         # NaN (no data in the window) is not equal to itself
        fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[start, end], y=[avg, avg], mode="lines", name=name + ", average",
                                 legendgroup=name, showlegend=False,
                                 line=dict(color=COLORS[name], width=3, dash="dot")))
    return avg
```

```{python}
def trade_balance_world(countries=("U.S.",), start=1976, end=2024):
    """Fig. 19.2 for any economies: the trade balance (% of GDP, WDI) and its average from start to end."""
    start, end = min(start, end), max(start, end)          # in case the sliders cross
    rows = world[world.country.isin(countries)]
    fig = px.line(rows, x="year", y="trade_balance", color="country", hover_name="country",
                  color_discrete_map=COLORS, labels={"year": "Year", "trade_balance": "Percent of GDP"})
    fig.update_traces(line_width=3)
    names = []
    for name in sorted(set(rows.country)):
        avg = add_average(fig, rows[rows.country == name].set_index("year").trade_balance, name, start, end)
        if avg == avg:
            names.append(f"{name} {round(avg, 1) + 0.0:+.1f}%")     # + 0.0 turns -0.0 into 0.0
        else:
            names.append(f"{name}: no data")
    more = f" + {len(names) - 2} more" if len(names) > 2 else ""
    fig.update_layout(title=f"Average trade balance {start}–{end}: " + ", ".join(names[:2]) + more,
                      legend_title_text="")
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_dash="dash", line_color="black", line_width=1)
    fig.add_vrect(x0=start, x1=end, fillcolor=GRAY, opacity=0.15, line_width=0)
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[1955, 2027])         # 1960 sits away from the corner
    fig.update_yaxes(range=fit_range(rows.trade_balance.dropna(), [-6.5, 2.5]))
    return fig
```
